idiom_name: explicit interface + precise types ([[nodiscard]], chrono, enum class, string_view)
implementation_notes: The Core Guidelines ask for an explicit interface (I.1) whose types are precise and strongly typed (I.4: 'Types are the simplest and best documentation'), so what replaces a prose-documented abstract interface is the declaration itself: `std::chrono::milliseconds timeout` instead of `int timeout_ms`, `enum class` instead of a set of booleans, `std::string_view` instead of `const char*`, `[[nodiscard]]` on queries, and named constructors (a static `Order::forCart(...)`) where a parameter list cannot state the intent. The call site then reads as the promise, and changing the representation cannot break clients. Keep the classic documented-base-class form where a released binary ABI must be preserved (Pimpl, I.27) or where the header must stay C-compatible (I.26).
pitfalls: Strong types must be cheap or nobody will use them: prefer `enum class`, `std::chrono`, `std::string_view` or a single-member struct with inline operations over a wrapper that allocates or copies.
A `[[nodiscard]]` query that lazily mutates, caches or performs I/O makes the name a lie and breaks `const` expectations - keep queries side-effect-free or name the operation as a command.
Preconditions written as comments rather than `Expects()`/`Ensures()` (or C++20 contracts) drift from the code, so the interface promises what it cannot enforce.

variants.name: Concept-constrained interfaces (Core Guidelines I.9)
variants.idiom_name: named concepts as the interface contract
variants.implementation_notes: I.9 tells you to document a template interface's requirements using concepts; with C++20 those requirements become checkable instead of prose, so the interface itself names the role an argument must play: `template <ShippingPolicy Policy> ...` rejects anything that cannot play that role, and a caller can read the concept instead of the body. The contract is declared, not described - which is why this realization is declarative rather than a documented abstract interface. Use it for template APIs whose constraints are stable enough to be named; keep unconstrained templates (with Doxygen preconditions) while the requirements are still moving or while the library must build with C++17 toolchains.
pitfalls: A concept that restates a single member function adds a name without removing a question - name the constraint after the role (`ShippingPolicy`), not after the syntax.
Concept errors are read by humans at the call site: an over-constrained concept (extra requirements nobody needs) makes the interface look harder to satisfy than it is.

On a pre-C++20 toolchain the concept does not parse at all, so the same interface silently degrades to an unconstrained template plus prose documentation - if the library must build with C++17, plan the fallback deliberately instead of discovering it in CI.
